metadata.subject: Data Structures
metadata.title: Discover Hash Tables
metadata.description: Map keys into buckets and see how chaining handles collisions.

learning_objectives: Calculate a deterministic bucket with key % table size.

mission.title: Map keys to buckets
mission.description: Use one simple hash rule and watch a collision form a chain.

introduction.title: A hash table gives a key a bucket
introduction.content: A hash function turns a key into a small bucket number, making it quick to find where the key belongs.
points: We use key % 5 as the rule.
A bucket can hold more than one key.
That shared bucket is called a collision.

worked_example.title: A collision is not an error
worked_example.content: Two keys can produce the same bucket number.

steps.explanation: 22 collides with 17, so chaining stores both keys in bucket 2.

worked_example.conclusion: The hash rule finds the bucket; chaining keeps colliding keys together.

next.title: Now build a table.
next.content: Insert the keys and watch each bucket.

next-step: The remainder tells us the bucket number.
This key joins a chain because the bucket is already occupied.
Every key now has a predictable bucket.

quiz.question: If table size is 5, which bucket receives key 22?

discovery.title: Hash Table discovery
discovery.summary: A hash function chooses a bucket, and chaining preserves keys that collide in the same bucket.

sections.title: What?
sections.content: A hash table maps a key to a bucket for quick lookup.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: 17 % 5 and 22 % 5 both equal 2, so they share bucket 2.

sections.title: Why?
sections.content: Chaining keeps collisions instead of losing either key.

sections.title: Remember
sections.content: Key → hash rule → bucket → chain if needed.

alternate_explanations.title: Think of mailboxes
alternate_explanations.content: A hash rule chooses a mailbox number; letters with the same number wait together in that mailbox.

recall.title: Recall
recall.prompt: In your own words, why can two keys appear in the same hash-table bucket?
recall.model_answer: Two different keys can produce the same hash result. Chaining stores both keys together in that bucket.
